title: Attention & Transformer Architecture
summary: Self-attention and the full Transformer block — the single most important architecture in modern AI.

slides.subTitle: A fixed-size context vector in old seq2seq models
slides.markdown: Before attention, seq2seq models (encoder-decoder RNNs) compressed an entire input sentence into **one fixed-size vector** — the encoder's final hidden state — and the decoder had to generate the whole output from that single vector. For short sentences this worked; for long ones, it didn't: information from early words got diluted or overwritten by the time the RNN reached the end, so translation quality degraded sharply as sentence length grew. The fix that started the whole line of research: let the decoder look back at **all** encoder hidden states, not just the last one, and learn which ones matter for each output word. That mechanism is attention.

slides.subTitle: Query, key, value — intuitively
slides.markdown: Attention answers: "for this position, which other positions should I pay attention to, and how much?" Every token produces three vectors: a **query** (what am I looking for), a **key** (what do I contain, for others to match against), and a **value** (what do I actually return if picked). A token's query is compared against every other token's key (via dot product) to get similarity scores; those scores are softmaxed into weights; the output is the weighted sum of all values using those weights. Concretely, in "the animal didn't cross the street because **it** was tired", the query for "it" scores highly against the key for "animal", so "it"'s output vector ends up heavily weighted toward "animal"'s value — resolving the reference without any explicit parsing rule.

slides.subTitle: A weighted context for one token
slides.markdown:
Self-attention means queries, keys, and values all come from the **same** sequence — every token attends to every other token in its own input, including itself. The diagram shows one token's query being scored against all keys, producing attention weights that are used to blend all the values into that token's new, context-aware representation.

![One query token attending to all key tokens, producing softmax weights that blend the value vectors](assets/self-attention.svg)

slides.subTitle: Why several attention "views" beat one
slides.markdown: A single attention computation forces all relationship types (syntactic, coreference, positional) to share one set of weights. **Multi-head attention** runs several attention computations in parallel, each with its own learned query/key/value projections, so different heads can specialize — one head might track subject-verb agreement, another might track coreference like "it" → "animal". The outputs of all heads are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model's dimension. This is why you'll see "8 heads" or "12 heads" in Transformer configs: it's not more attention *computation* in total (each head works in a smaller subspace), it's more attention *diversity*.

slides.subTitle: Injecting order into an order-blind mechanism
slides.markdown: Self-attention itself has no notion of order — it computes the same set of pairwise scores regardless of token position, meaning "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would attend identically without help. **Positional encoding** adds a position-dependent vector to each token's embedding before it enters the attention layers, typically fixed sinusoidal functions of different frequencies (in the original Transformer) or learned position embeddings (in BERT/GPT). This gives the model a way to distinguish "token 1" from "token 5" while still letting attention itself remain permutation-based and fully parallel — order is injected as *input*, not baked into the mechanism.

slides.subTitle: Attention, feedforward, residuals, normalization
slides.markdown:
One Transformer block stacks: multi-head self-attention → add the block's input back in (**residual connection**) → **layer normalization** → a position-wise feedforward network → another residual connection → another layer norm. Residuals let gradients flow directly through many stacked blocks without vanishing; layer norm stabilizes the scale of activations between sub-layers. Stacking dozens of these identical blocks (12 in BERT-base, 96 in GPT-3) is what gives Transformers their depth and capacity.

![A Transformer block showing multi-head attention and feedforward sub-layers, each wrapped with a residual connection and layer normalization](assets/transformer-block.svg)

slides.subTitle: Encoder-only vs decoder-only vs encoder-decoder
slides.markdown: **Encoder-only** (BERT): every token attends to every other token, both directions — best for understanding tasks (classification, NER) where you have the full input up front. **Decoder-only** (GPT): each token can only attend to earlier tokens (causal masking) — the natural fit for open-ended generation, since it's exactly how autoregressive text generation works. **Encoder-decoder** (T5, the original Transformer): an encoder builds a bidirectional representation of the input, and a decoder generates output while cross-attending to that representation — the fit for sequence-to-sequence tasks like translation, where input and output are genuinely different sequences.

slides.subTitle: Parallel training and long-range dependencies
slides.markdown:
| | RNN/LSTM | Transformer |
|---|---|---|
| Processing | Sequential, step-by-step | All positions processed in parallel |
| Training speed | Slow — can't parallelize across time steps | Fast — attention is one big matrix multiply |
| Long-range dependencies | Degrade with distance (even with LSTM gating) | Direct — any two tokens are one attention hop apart |
| Cost at long sequence length | Linear in sequence length | Quadratic in sequence length |

The practical decision: Transformers win almost everywhere training throughput and long-range context matter, which is most modern NLP — RNNs remain relevant mainly for streaming/low-latency settings or extremely long sequences where quadratic cost is prohibitive.

slides.subTitle: Why long context is expensive
slides.markdown: It's easy to assume Transformers scale like RNNs — they don't. Self-attention computes a score between **every pair** of tokens, so compute and memory scale as O(n²) in sequence length n. Doubling the context window from 1k to 2k tokens roughly **quadruples** the attention cost, not doubles it. This is the real reason "just give it a longer context window" isn't free — it's why techniques like sparse attention, sliding-window attention, and linear-attention approximations exist, and why context-window increases in production LLMs are treated as a major engineering effort, not a config flag.

slides.subTitle: The core computation in ~10 lines
slides.markdown:
The formula behind every attention layer, as pseudocode:

```python
def scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V):
    # Q, K, V: [seq_len, d_k]
    scores = Q @ K.T                # [seq_len, seq_len] similarity
    scores = scores / sqrt(d_k)     # scale to stop softmax saturating
    weights = softmax(scores, axis=-1)
    return weights @ V              # weighted blend of values
```

The `/ sqrt(d_k)` scaling matters more than it looks: without it, dot products grow large as dimension `d_k` grows, pushing softmax into a near-one-hot regime with vanishing gradients — the "scaled" in the name isn't cosmetic, it's what keeps training stable.
